chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a person in Ihram who killed a wasp. He said: 'If it was by mistake, there is nothing upon him.' I said: 'No, but it was deliberate.' He said: 'He should feed something from food.' I said: 'If it intended (to attack) me?' He said: 'Everything which intends (to attack) you, so kill it.'

key_terms.مُحْرِمٍ: One in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.يُطْعِمُ: He feeds (referring to the expiation of feeding the poor)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a person in Ihram who kills a wasp?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi clarifies the distinction between accidental and deliberate killing of a wasp (zumburah) during Ihram, establishing that intentional killing incurs a light expiation of feeding food, while defensive killing against an attacker is exempt. It highlights the Shia juristic principle of 'intention' (iradah) in determining liability, where the wasp's aggressive intent justifies immediate killing without penalty, reflecting the practical flexibility in Ihram regulations.
